name: EMCOR Group, Inc.
employees: ~44,000 (31 December 2025; all in the United States after the UK sale — about 62% union under roughly 450 collective bargaining agreements); ~40,400 a year earlier

ownership.notes: Delaware corporation; Commission file 1-8267; fiscal year ends 31 December. 44,109,901 shares outstanding at 2026-07-24; non-affiliate market value about USD 17.26bn at 2025-06-30. Holders above 5%: BlackRock 8.03% and FMR 5.94% (2026 proxy); Vanguard disclaimed beneficial ownership in a March 2026 13G/A. Directors and officers together hold 0.73%.

summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: EMCOR is the largest US mechanical and electrical construction and facilities-services contractor — FY2025 revenue USD 16.99bn, record remaining performance obligations of USD 17.14bn at 30 June 2026 (up 43.9% in a year) — and the data-centre build is now its largest end market: the network and communications sector produced USD 973m of electrical and USD 799m of mechanical revenue in Q2 2026 alone, 58% and 35% of those segments, up from 50% and 22% a year earlier. Management raised FY2026 guidance twice to USD 20.0–20.5bn of revenue and USD 32.00–33.25 of diluted EPS after beating consensus by 25% in Q2. BACKGROUND. Norwalk, Connecticut; about 100 operating subsidiaries and 44,000 employees, 62% union; four US segments after the December 2025 sale of the UK business (USD 256.6m net proceeds, USD 144.9m gain). It bought Miller Electric (Jacksonville; ESOP-owned since 2012) for USD 865m cash on 3 February 2025 — USD 1.09bn of 2025 revenue — and five further electrical contractors in 2026 for USD 750m upfront (B&B, Sidney, Connelly, Giles, Schmidt; about USD 625m of trailing revenue). ENR ranks it second among specialty contractors behind Quanta (2024 revenue USD 14.57bn); EC&M ranks its electrical business third (USD 5.1bn of 2025 sales) behind Quanta and Rosendin. Filings name no customer; the chief executive says the data-centre customers are 'who you would think they would be' — the major cloud operators — across '17 electrical and seven mechanical data center markets'. Collection gap: network-and-communications RPO is disclosed only as a chart (about USD 4.46bn, 33% of total, at end-2025 per the Q4 call); the UK buyer is unnamed; no hyperscaler is named in any filing or call.
ecosystemRole: We assess EMCOR as a build-segment incumbent on the record of two rankers — ENR's No. 2 specialty contractor and EC&M's No. 3 electrical contractor — and the one covered contractor that self-performs both the electrical and the mechanical scope of a data hall at scale: the switchgear, UPS and distribution on one side, the chilled-water plant, piping, air handling and fire protection on the other, with fabrication shops of up to 250,000 sq ft feeding them. In this corpus it is the largest procurement channel into the AIDC supply chain among specialty contractors, buying equipment and materials under its own purchase orders for fixed-price and GMP contracts, and the clearest public read on data-centre construction demand each quarter through its market-sector table.

productsAndServices.name: US electrical construction and facilities services
productsAndServices.category: Segment · USD 5.07bn FY2025 revenue (30%), 12.1% operating margin
productsAndServices.description: Design, integration, installation, start-up and maintenance of 'systems for electrical power transmission, distribution, and generation, including power cables, conduits, distribution panels, transformers, generators, uninterruptible power supply systems, and related switch gear and controls', premises electrical and lighting, low-voltage fire-alarm, security and process control, voice and data cabling, solar and EV-charging installation, and transit signalling — delivered through subsidiaries including Miller Electric (Florida and the Southeast), the Dynalectric companies (Arizona, Oregon, Colorado, Nevada, Ohio, San Diego and the Washington DC division in Sterling, Virginia), Forest Electric (New York and New Jersey), Gibson Electric, Baker Electric and the five 2026 acquisitions. Network and communications — 'including data centers, data and fiber projects, and cabling' — was 48% of segment revenue in FY2025 (USD 2,461.9m) and 58% in Q2 2026 (USD 973.0m).
highlights: Q2 2026: revenue USD 1,662.5m (+24.0%), operating income USD 231.4m, margin 13.9% (11.8% a year earlier); RPO USD 6.27bn at 30 June 2026 (USD 3.07bn at end-2024)

FY2025 margin dipped to 12.1% from 13.4% on 'lower profitability on certain projects in new geographies where we encountered reduced labor productivity or availability while investing in the development of a workforce' plus about 80 bp of Miller amortisation
Miller Electric contributed USD 1.09bn of 2025 revenue and about USD 1.0bn of RPO at acquisition; Dynalectric's DC division employs about 2,500 in Loudoun County's data-centre market (trade press)

Guzzi: 'We operate in 17 electrical and seven mechanical data center markets and expect to add a few more'; roughly 'two-thirds of the electrical division's total quarterly revenue growth' in Q1 2026 came from data centres (Zacks)
productsAndServices.positioning: EC&M's No. 3 electrical contractor on 2025 sales of USD 5.1bn (+42.5%), behind Quanta (USD 23.0bn) and Rosendin (USD 5.5bn) and ahead of Everus, MYR, IES, M.C. Dean, MMR and Faith Technologies; the 10-K names APi, Comfort Systems, Dycom, Everus, IES, MasTec, MYR, Quanta and Tutor Perini as competitors. Differentiation is union craft that 'will travel themselves' into rural campus markets, a decentralised subsidiary model that keeps local supervision, and the mechanical scope under the same roof.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct contracts with owners and developers and as subcontractor to general contractors and construction managers; 'a majority of our revenues are derived from projects requiring competitive bids'; fixed-price, GMP and cost-plus contracts
targetSegments: Network and communications (data centres) — 48% of FY2025 segment revenue
productsAndServices.roadmap: Five 2026 electrical acquisitions (about USD 625m of trailing revenue; USD 250–275m expected in H2 2026); Q3 2026 results expected Thursday 29 October 2026 (inferred from cadence; no notice yet)

productsAndServices.name: US mechanical construction and facilities services
productsAndServices.category: Segment · USD 7.05bn FY2025 revenue (42%), 12.8% operating margin
productsAndServices.description: HVAC and refrigeration 'including both traditional mechanical systems as well as geothermal solutions', clean-room process ventilation, fire protection and suppression, 'plumbing, process and high-purity piping systems', controls and filtration, water and wastewater treatment, central plants 'including manufacturing and installing sheet metal air handling systems', millwright, and steel fabrication and erection — the scope that in a data hall covers the chilled-water plant, piping, air handling, fire protection and the liquid-cooling distribution. Subsidiaries with mission-critical practices include Upland Mechanical (250,000 sq ft fabrication facility), Batchelor & Kimball (90,000 sq ft prefabrication plant), Bahnson, Shambaugh & Son with Progressive Pipe Fabricators, Tucker Mechanical and the University Mechanical companies. Network and communications was 23% of segment revenue in FY2025 (USD 1,670.4m) and 35% in Q2 2026 (USD 799.3m), having 'more than doubled year-over-year'.
highlights: Q2 2026: revenue USD 2,300.9m (+31.1%), operating income USD 286.6m, margin 12.5% (13.6% a year earlier); RPO USD 9.37bn — 55% of the group total

The 110 bp margin decline in H1 2026 was 'a change in project mix' — more construction-manager and prime-contractor roles at lower margins and 'an increase in the number of guaranteed maximum price and cost plus contracts, particularly in newer geographies or on projects where design or scope is still evolving'
Guzzi: AI data centres carry 'a multiplier of 1.5 to 2' on mechanical scope versus traditional cloud builds, 'probably 1.5' on electrical

FY2025 gross profit gains came from 'investments in virtual design and construction, prefabrication, and automation… the most significant increase in gross profit coming from network and communications'
productsAndServices.positioning: The larger of the two construction segments and the one with the AI multiplier; competes with Comfort Systems USA (technology 58% of Q2 2026 revenue), APi and Southland rather than with the GCs. Of the covered EPC and GC set only EMCOR self-performs mechanical and electrical at this scale.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct owner contracts and subcontracts to general contractors; increasingly GMP and cost-plus where 'design is still changing'
targetSegments: High-tech manufacturing (semiconductor, biotech, EV chain) — USD 998m FY2025
productsAndServices.roadmap: Fabrication facilities 'leased with a payback target of three years or less'; capex growing 28–30% a year against 14–15% revenue growth (Laguna conference, September 2026)

productsAndServices.category: Segment · USD 3.12bn FY2025 revenue (18%), 6.0% operating margin
productsAndServices.description: Maintenance and repair of 'mechanical, electrical, plumbing, fire safety, and building automation systems', HVAC retrofits, energy-efficiency programmes, commercial and government site-based operations and facilities management; 77% mechanical services, 18% commercial site-based, 5% government site-based (NARA, FDIC, GAO and other federal buildings). highlights: Q2 2026: revenue USD 837.7m (+5.6%), operating income USD 63.4m, margin 7.6%
RPO USD 1.36bn at 30 June 2026; service RPO limited to notice periods where cancellable
Competes 'with entities such as APi Group Corporation, Comfort Systems USA, Inc., and Service Logic LLC, as well as Carrier Global Corporation and Trane Technologies plc' in mechanical services
productsAndServices.positioning: The recurring-revenue base under the construction cycle — the lifecycle layer FTI ON imitates at a fraction of the scale.

productsAndServices.name: US industrial services
productsAndServices.category: Segment · USD 1.27bn FY2025 revenue (7%), 2.0% operating margin
productsAndServices.description: Refinery and petrochemical turnarounds, specialty welding, overhaul of alkylation, cracking and coking units, design, manufacture and repair of shell-and-tube heat exchangers (Ohmstede), refractory and acid-proofing, and 'renewable energy services, including large scale solar projects, energy storage, and waste to biogas solutions'. Brands include Ohmstede, AltairStrickland, Repcon, Rabalais and MOR PPM.
highlights: Q2 2026: revenue USD 353.8m (+25.9%), operating income USD 9.6m (2.7%) after a loss-making Q2 2025; work-in-process rising on 'greater new build heat exchanger orders'
Guzzi (Q2 2026): the autumn turnaround season 'will not be as strong as it normally can be because of what's happening in the Middle East'
MSHA imminent-danger order to MOR PPM at the Sivells Bend mine, Texas, 28 July 2026 — no injuries (8-K)

productsAndServices.name: Acquisition programme — Miller Electric and the 2026 electrical roll-up
productsAndServices.description: EMCOR buys regional specialty contractors and leaves them under their own names and leaders. Miller Electric Company (Jacksonville, founded 1928; ESOP-owned since 2012) was bought from its ESOP trust and the Walden and Brown family trusts for USD 865m cash on 3 February 2025 (USD 876.8m after adjustments; about USD 805m of 2024 revenue, USD 80m of EBITDA, USD 755m of RPO at announcement; 90% of revenue in Florida and the Southeast; 'more than 1,000 clients in sectors like data centers, manufacturing, and healthcare'); it reports to Dan Fitzgibbons with Henry K. Brown remaining CEO. In 2026 five electrical contractors — B&B Electric (Wisconsin), Sidney Electric (Ohio), Connelly Electric (Illinois), Giles Electric (Daytona Beach, folded into Miller) and Schmidt Electric (Austin, 'data center focus') — were acquired for USD 750m upfront with up to USD 90m of earn-outs: about USD 625m of trailing revenue, USD 105m of EBITDA and 1,500 employees. Nine 2025 tuck-ins cost USD 182.1m.
highlights: Miller's 2025 contribution: USD 1.09bn of revenue and USD 21.3m of operating income after USD 40.5m of amortisation; intangibles USD 475m (customer relationships USD 280m over 16 years)
Miller's Flexential relationship spans five of six Atlanta sites plus Jacksonville, Tampa and Charlotte — 'white space fit-outs' (Miller's own news page)
The UK business (USD 471m of 2025 revenue) was sold on 1 December 2025 for USD 256.6m net, buyer unnamed; proceeds redirected to US M&A and prefabrication
Funding: cash on hand (USD 924m at 30 June 2026) and an undrawn revolver; total debt USD 6.1m
productsAndServices.positioning: The roll-up is explicitly geographic — 'low- and medium-voltage contractors to expand its geographic reach and strengthen market density' — buying the local supervision that Guzzi calls the real bottleneck rather than the labour brokers it refuses to use.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Not applicable — internal capital allocation (acquisitions, capex, dividends, buybacks roughly 50/50 since 2017)
targetSegments: Electrical contractors in Texas, the Midwest and the Southeast
productsAndServices.roadmap: Schmidt and Sidney were pending at 30 July 2026 and now appear on the EMCOR Construction roster; H2 2026 contribution USD 250–275m

strategyRead: 1. (High confidence) We assess that EMCOR's data-centre franchise is a two-trade position no covered peer matches: it installs both halves of the hall — the electrical chain from switchgear to UPS and the mechanical chain from chiller plant to liquid-cooling distribution — and the AI transition widens the mechanical half most. Basis: Q2 2026 network and communications revenue of USD 973m electrical and USD 799m mechanical; management's 1.5–2× mechanical multiplier; mechanical RPO at 55% of the USD 17.14bn total.

2. (High confidence) We assess that the strategy is to buy local supervision rather than to broker labour. Basis: Guzzi — 'we're not going to be the contractor that uses a labor broker'; 'our real bottleneck… is supervision'; Miller (USD 865m) and five 2026 electrical deals (USD 750m) all bought in the Southeast, Texas and the Midwest, left under their own names, with union craft that 'will travel themselves'. The acquisitions are geography and foremen, not technology.

3. (Moderate confidence) We assess that margin, not growth, is the next test. Basis: mechanical margin fell 110 bp in H1 2026 on more construction-manager roles and 'guaranteed maximum price and cost plus contracts… in newer geographies or on projects where design or scope is still evolving'; electrical margin was hit in 2025 by productivity in new geographies and a fixed-price 'challenged project' in a new market. Guidance of 9.5–9.8% assumes the mix stabilises; a second challenged project would reprice the stock faster than a revenue miss.

4. (Moderate confidence) We assess that the stock's repeated post-beat sell-offs (January 2025, October 2025, February and June 2026) reflect concentration pricing rather than operating doubt. Basis: electrical grew 52% while other segments grew single digits in Q3 2025; sell-side puts data centres at about 30% of backlog and 33% of US construction revenue; the company itself names a decline in data-centre capital spending as its first demand risk. Holders are paying for a cycle and exit on any sign it is slowing.

5. (Moderate confidence) We assess that EMCOR's visibility is lengthening with project size and that this cuts both ways. Basis: RPO completed within twelve months fell from about 85% to 75–76%, and in-year bookings from about 60% to 40–45% of RPO (management and Zacks). Longer, larger campus contracts mean two to three years of visibility — and more exposure to owner pauses, power delays and the local moratoria EC&M's 2026 survey calls a new risk factor.

6. (Low confidence) We assess that the industrial-services renewables line (solar, energy storage, biogas) will remain immaterial to the AIDC chain. Basis: the 10-K names it without a figure, the segment earns 2–3% margins, and no storage project is disclosed; EMCOR's relevance to battery sellers runs through the data-hall UPS and the generator-paralleling scope, not through a storage EPC practice.

relationships.note: Named competitor in the 10-K; ENR's No. 1 specialty contractor (USD 23.67bn) to EMCOR's No. 2 (USD 14.57bn); EC&M No. 1 to No. 3.
relationships.context: The 10-K lists Quanta among 'larger companies focused on providing electrical and/or mechanical construction services'. On ENR's 2025 Top 600 Quanta led with USD 23,672.8m of 2024 revenue against EMCOR's USD 14,566.1m; on EC&M's 2026 table Quanta's USD 23.0bn of electrical sales is 4.5 times EMCOR's USD 5.1bn. Quanta's franchise is transmission and utility; EMCOR's is inside the building.

relationships.note: EC&M 2026 No. 2 (USD 5.5bn, +49%) immediately above EMCOR's electrical business (No. 3, USD 5.1bn, +42%).
relationships.context: Rosendin is the one private electrical contractor larger than EMCOR's electrical segment and, like EMCOR, union and prefabrication-led; it publishes a 15 GW data-centre record where EMCOR discloses only sector revenue. The two meet on hyperscale electrical packages in Virginia, Texas and Arizona.

relationships.note: Named competitor in the 10-K; MasTec's record USD 21.4bn backlog (Q2 2026) is the peer figure analysts set beside EMCOR's USD 17.14bn RPO.
relationships.context: Listed in the same 10-K competitor sentence as Quanta; Zacks pairs the two on backlog. MasTec's data-centre exposure is outside-the-fence (power and communications infrastructure) where EMCOR's is inside the hall.

relationships.note: Named competitor in mechanical services ('Carrier Global Corporation and Trane Technologies plc'); also the kind of OEM whose equipment EMCOR's mechanical subsidiaries install.
relationships.context: The 10-K places Trane among the competitors to EMCOR's mechanical-services division alongside APi, Comfort Systems and Service Logic. No supply agreement is disclosed; the relationship on data-centre projects is installer-to-OEM in practice and competitor in service.

relationships.note: EC&M 2026 No. 9 (USD 2.28bn, +62.6%) — the merit-shop prefabrication-led rival to EMCOR's union electrical subsidiaries.
relationships.context: Both name supervision and prefabrication as the constraint and the answer; FTI's five new 500,000 sq ft plants and ABC's No. 1 data-centre ranking by hours contrast with EMCOR's leased fabrication shops and union craft. They compete for the same hyperscale electrical packages in the Southeast and Midwest.
A passive index holding reported in the 2026 proxy; FMR holds 5.94% and Vanguard disclaimed beneficial ownership in March 2026.

relationships.note: Historical: Dynalectric Colorado and Trautman & Shreve performed electrical and mechanical work on Xilinx's Longmont data-centre expansion (Xilinx is now part of AMD).
relationships.context: Data Center Dynamics reported the two EMCOR subsidiaries teaming on the Xilinx Longmont expansion before AMD's 2022 acquisition of Xilinx; the page is behind a script wall and its date was not retrievable. Recorded as a historical reference, not a current engagement.

policyExposure.exposure: The 10-K warns that 'changes in U.S. foreign trade policies could lead to the imposition of additional trade barriers and tariffs', that 'certain of our fixed price contracts do not allow us to adjust our prices and, as a result, increases in material costs could reduce our profitability', and that judicial review of executive-order tariffs could reverse policies again. No Section 232 or 301 line is named and no tariff cost is quantified; inventories rose in 2026 on 'advanced purchases of materials and equipment… to mitigate the impact of long lead times'.
policyExposure.mitigation: Management states it will 'pass on price increases and protect ourselves through favorable contractual terms' and manage tariffs as it managed COVID-era supply disruption.

policyExposure.regime: CHIPS and Science Act and Inflation Reduction Act appropriations
policyExposure.exposure: 'Our business may be adversely affected by… the failure to fully fund or implement legislation such as the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 and the Inflation Reduction Act' — the high-tech manufacturing sector (semiconductor, biotech, EV chain) fell to USD 998m of mechanical revenue in 2025 from USD 1,453m in 2024 as fab and EV programmes slowed. No 45X or credit-transfer exposure is stated.

About 62% of employees are union under roughly 450 collective bargaining agreements and the company contributes to about 200 multiemployer pension plans; the 10-K states that 'our potential liability for unfunded liabilities could be material' on withdrawal. The union model is also the stated competitive advantage in rural campus markets.

policyExposure.regime: Local data-centre moratoria and power availability
policyExposure.exposure: The 10-K names 'the availability or price of electricity' as a risk to customers' data-centre buildouts; Guzzi (Q2 2026) says the company works where owners 'have power and they're willing to build power' — Virginia and Texas first — and that moratoria are 'difficult to maintain long term' given county tax revenues; EC&M's 2026 survey records moratoriums and permitting delays as a new risk factor for three-quarters of top electrical contractors.

decisionMakers.name: Anthony J. (Tony) Guzzi
decisionMakers.title: Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer
background: CEO since January 2011; President since October 2004 (COO 2004–2011); Chairman since June 2018; director since December 2009; age 61
President, North American Distribution and Aftermarket Division, Carrier Corporation (from August 2001); earlier engagement manager at McKinsey & Company
Lead director of Hubbell Incorporated; co-founder of the Johnny Mac Soldiers Fund; 2025 total compensation USD 14,380,630; owns 170,299 shares
On the model: 'We're not going to be the contractor that uses a labor broker and places labor around the country'; 'our real bottleneck… is supervision'

decisionMakers.name: Jason R. Nalbandian
decisionMakers.title: Senior Vice President, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Accounting Officer
background: CFO since April 2024 (succeeding Mark A. Pompa); SVP and CAO since January 2022; Controller 2019–2022; joined May 2014 as Director of Accounting and Analysis; age 38
Previously Ernst & Young assurance practice; CPA; BS and MS in accounting, Fairfield University

decisionMakers.name: Maxine L. Mauricio
decisionMakers.title: Executive Vice President, Chief Administrative Officer, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary
background: General Counsel and Secretary since January 2016; EVP since February 2021; CAO since December 2023; joined 2002 as Assistant General Counsel from Ropes & Gray; age 54
Dartmouth BA; Harvard JD; director of Novanta Inc.

decisionMakers.name: Daniel Fitzgibbons
decisionMakers.title: President and Chief Executive Officer, EMCOR Electrical Construction Services
background: Miller Electric and the 2026 electrical acquisitions report to him; 'actively involved in EMCOR's acquisition program'

More than 35 years in the electrical industry 'with a specialty in communications and technology'; co-founded Communications & Data Services in 1992 (acquired by Gibson Electric 1998); President and CEO of Gibson Electric for 13 years from 2006
On Miller: 'By leveraging advanced technologies such as virtual design and construction, along with prefabrication techniques, they have a proven record of continually improving project efficiency'

decisionMakers.name: Brian D. Batchelor
decisionMakers.title: President and Chief Executive Officer, EMCOR Mechanical Construction Services
background: Former CEO of Batchelor & Kimball (Conyers, Georgia), which he 'grew fourfold… developing their manufacturing and fabrication capabilities' — the 90,000 sq ft prefabrication plant that now serves data centres
Earlier Johnson Controls engineer and Jones Day attorney; Vanderbilt BSME; Emory MBA and JD

decisionMakers.name: Henry K. Brown
decisionMakers.title: Chief Executive Officer, Miller Electric Company
background: Retained as CEO after the February 2025 sale; seller-side representative in the stock purchase agreement and beneficiary of the Henry K. Brown Trust I; Daniel A. Brown is Chairman and Ed Witt Jr. President and COO

'Joining forces with EMCOR will allow us to further enhance our services… in the evolving energy and infrastructure landscape' (January 2025); Miller's Brian Yarber is Vice President of Data Center Services

periods.commentary: Network and communications revenue rose 45% in electrical and more than doubled in mechanical. H1 2026 operating cash flow of USD 289.9m against USD 302.2m a year earlier reflects working capital on 'strong organic revenue growth'.
